title: The swollen eyelid that hurts to move
stem: A 13-year-old boy has three days of worsening left eyelid swelling and frontal headache, after a week of purulent nasal discharge. Temperature 38.4 °C. BVA 20/20 OD, 20/40 OS. Mild left RAPD, red saturation 60% OS, 3 mm proptosis, tense chemosis, painful restriction of elevation and abduction. IOP 17 OD, 27 OS. Cornea clear, chamber quiet, fundus normal.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Preseptal cellulitis with reactive chemosis
Idiopathic orbital inflammatory syndrome
Cavernous sinus thrombosis complicating sinusitis
Orbital cellulitis of ethmoid sinus origin
Orbital rhabdomyosarcoma with secondary inflammation

items.why: Proptosis, painful restricted motility, RAPD, reduced colour and acuity, and raised IOP all place the disease behind the septum. Fever with a week of purulent rhinorrhoea names the source.

dis.label: Cavernous sinus thrombosis
dis.tempting: The correct escalation of this infection, and it also gives proptosis and chemosis.
dis.ruled: Signs stay strictly unilateral, with no multiple cranial neuropathy and no V1-V2 loss.

dis.label: Preseptal cellulitis
dis.tempting: The visible finding is a swollen lid, and preseptal disease is commoner at this age.
dis.ruled: Preseptal disease spares acuity, pupil, colour, motility and globe position.

dis.label: Rhabdomyosarcoma
dis.tempting: Rapid proptosis in a child is the classic teaching phrase for it.
dis.ruled: Fever and purulent sinus disease over three days fit infection, not tumour.

items.q: Which three findings measure optic nerve function, rather than supporting the infective diagnosis?

options.t: Temperature 38.4 °C
Left relative afferent pupillary defect
Red saturation reduced to 60% OS
Purulent nasal discharge for one week
Intraocular pressure 27 mmHg OS
Best corrected acuity 20/40 OS

items.why: The item asks for afferent function, not for evidence of infection. An RAPD, dyschromatopsia and reduced best acuity each measure optic nerve conduction directly.

dis.label: IOP 27 mmHg
dis.tempting: It is genuinely abnormal, and orbital pressure is what threatens the nerve.
dis.ruled: It measures orbital pressure, not conduction. Normalising it proves nothing.

dis.label: Fever, purulent discharge
dis.tempting: They confirm infection and drive the diagnosis.
dis.ruled: Neither measures the eye. A febrile child can have a normal afferent system.

items.q: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.t: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate, nasal decongestant, review in 24 hours
Same-day referral for contrast CT, intravenous antibiotics, ophthalmology and ENT
Outpatient MRI within 48 hours, then decide about admission
Intravenous antibiotics booked for the morning, oral cover overnight
Oral corticosteroid with a topical antibiotic to settle the swelling

items.short: Same-day referral, contrast CT, IV antibiotics
items.why: Orbital cellulitis with afferent dysfunction threatens the eye and, through intracranial extension, life. Imaging, intravenous therapy and surgical availability are arranged together, today.

dis.label: IV antibiotics tomorrow
dis.tempting: It sees that intravenous therapy is needed and feels like a fair compromise.
dis.ruled: The overnight delay is where vision goes. The decision point is the RAPD, now.

dis.label: Outpatient MRI in 48 hours
dis.tempting: MRI is the better soft-tissue study, so it reads as the more thorough answer.
dis.ruled: Contrast CT answers today's questions faster: sinus, collection, apex, bone.

items.q: Which anatomic route most commonly explains this presentation?

options.t: Direct spread across the lamina papyracea from the ethmoid sinus
Retrograde thrombophlebitis through valveless facial and orbital veins
Extension through the optic canal from the sphenoid sinus
Ascending infection along the nasolacrimal duct from the inferior meatus
Haematogenous seeding of the orbit from an occult bacteraemia

items.why: The medial orbital wall is paper-thin and perforated by vessels, which makes contiguous ethmoid spread the usual route and explains why abduction and elevation fail first.

dis.label: Valveless venous spread
dis.tempting: A real mechanism, and how mid-face infection reaches the cavernous sinus.
dis.ruled: Not the usual route from sinusitis, and it does not localise medially.

dis.label: Optic canal, sphenoid
dis.tempting: Sphenoid disease is dangerous and sits against the orbital apex.
dis.ruled: Rare in children, and it would show apical signs before medial restriction.

items.q: He is admitted on intravenous antibiotics. Which change over 18 hours most supports drainage?

options.t: Temperature settles after two doses while the lid oedema persists
CT shows a 4 mm medial subperiosteal collection, acuity improving
Acuity falls to 20/80 with worse colour and an abscess crowding the apex
Blood cultures grow an organism fully sensitive to current therapy
Chemosis increases while pupil, colour and acuity stay unchanged

items.short: Falling function with an apical abscess
items.why: Drainage is driven by function and location, not by the presence of a collection. Falling afferent function with apical involvement is the indication, as is failure to improve on adequate therapy.

dis.label: Abscess, function improving
dis.tempting: An abscess on imaging feels like a surgical finding by definition.
dis.ruled: Small medial collections often resolve on antibiotics. Imaging does not decide.

dis.label: Chemosis increasing
dis.tempting: It looks like deterioration in front of you.
dis.ruled: Surface swelling with unchanged afferent function is no reason to open an orbit.

rules: If lid swelling comes with any change in acuity, colour, pupil, motility or globe position, treat it as orbital until imaging says otherwise. If function falls, drain.

rows: Crosses to the other eye within hours to days
Motility limited by swelling and pain
III, IV, VI and V1-V2 out of proportion to swelling
RAPD if the apex is crowded
RAPD plus a poorly reactive mid-dilated pupil
pair.decider: Bilateral signs, or multiple cranial neuropathies out of proportion to orbital swelling, mean cavernous sinus and neurosurgical admission rather than orbital drainage.

title: The pain that woke a lens wearer at four in the morning
stem: A 24-year-old woman wears monthly silicone hydrogel lenses, sleeps in them twice a week, and tops up the solution in her case rather than discarding it. Pain, photophobia and green discharge for 36 hours OS. BVA 20/25 OD, 20/200 OS. A 2.2 mm paracentral epithelial defect over a dense stromal infiltrate, 1.2 mm hypopyon, circumlimbal injection, stromal oedema. IOP 14 OD, 11 OS.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Contact lens induced sterile peripheral ulcer
Pseudomonas keratitis related to overnight wear
Adenoviral keratitis with subepithelial infiltrates
Acanthamoeba keratitis in a topping-up lens user
Marginal staphylococcal hypersensitivity keratitis

items.why: A large epithelial defect over a dense suppurative infiltrate, with hypopyon and mucopurulent discharge inside 36 hours, is bacterial. Sleeping in lenses and topped-up solution point to Pseudomonas.

dis.label: Sterile CLPU
dis.tempting: Also lens related, also painful, and commoner than infection in this group.
dis.ruled: CLPU is small, peripheral, without hypopyon, and the epithelium stays intact.

dis.label: Acanthamoeba keratitis
dis.tempting: Poor solution hygiene is the classic risk factor quoted for it.
dis.ruled: Onset in 36 hours with hypopyon and pus is too fast and too suppurative.

items.q: Which three steps belong in the first hour of management?

options.t: Corneal scrape for Gram stain and culture before drops start
Hourly topical fluoroquinolone monotherapy, day and night
Send the lens, case and solution for culture as well
Topical dexamethasone four times daily to limit scarring
Topical antifungal cover pending microscopy results
Pressure patch after cycloplegia for pain relief

items.short: Scrape and culture, hourly quinolone, lens culture
items.why: Culture is taken before the first drop, because therapy sterilises the plate within hours. Hourly fluoroquinolone covers Pseudomonas, and lens, case and solution often grow the same organism.

dis.label: Topical steroid now
dis.tempting: Scarring is the long-term risk, and steroid does reduce stromal infiltrate.
dis.ruled: Steroid before the organism is known and controlled invites rapid melt.

dis.label: Antifungal, patching
dis.tempting: Both feel cautious: broad cover, and comfort for a very painful eye.
dis.ruled: No fungal risk factor here, and patching an infected cornea incubates it.

items.q: She is reviewed at 48 hours. Which finding most justifies changing therapy?

options.t: The infiltrate is denser with 0.4 mm more stromal thinning
Culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa fully sensitive to ciprofloxacin
Pain is worse although the epithelial defect has shrunk by half
The hypopyon has settled and the anterior chamber is quieter
Injection persists and she complains of stinging on the drops

items.why: Response is judged on infiltrate density, defect size and thinning, not on symptoms or the sensitivity report. Progressive thinning on adequate cover means fortified drops and a perforation plan.

dis.label: Sensitive on culture
dis.tempting: It confirms the drug choice, which reads like the decision point.
dis.ruled: Sensitivity in a dish says nothing about the cornea in front of you.

dis.label: Worse pain, smaller defect
dis.tempting: Pain is what she reports, so it feels like the outcome measure.
dis.ruled: Pain lags healing. A defect halving on hourly drops is progress.

items.q: Which addition best manages her pain and anterior chamber reaction?

options.t: Topical cyclopentolate 1% twice daily with oral analgesia
Topical ketorolac four times daily with oral analgesia
Subconjunctival gentamicin with topical anaesthetic
Topical atropine 1% twice daily and a bandage lens
Oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for three days

items.why: Cycloplegia relieves ciliary spasm and limits synechiae without touching epithelial healing or host defence. Analgesia is oral, because topical anaesthetic delays healing and masks progression.

dis.label: Subconjunctival gentamicin
dis.tempting: It puts potent Gram-negative cover straight at the site.
dis.ruled: Hourly drops already give high corneal levels, and this adds needle risk.

dis.label: Topical NSAID
dis.tempting: It treats pain and inflammation without steroid, which sounds safe.
dis.ruled: Topical NSAIDs are linked to melt in a cornea that is already thinning.

items.q: Which organism factor best explains the speed of stromal destruction?

options.t: Secreted proteases and elastase that digest stromal collagen
Biofilm formation on the lens surface and in the storage case
Endotoxin release driving neutrophil chemotaxis into the stroma
Adhesion to compromised epithelium through pili and flagella
Cyst formation that resists disinfection by the solution

items.why: Pseudomonas secretes proteases and elastase that cleave stromal collagen directly, which is why melting is measured in hours. Biofilm and adhesion explain how it arrived, not the speed.

dis.label: Biofilm on lens and case
dis.tempting: Biofilm is why topping up solution fails, and it is genuinely present.
dis.ruled: It explains inoculation and persistence, not the rate of stromal loss.

dis.label: Cyst formation
dis.tempting: Resistance to disinfection fits the hygiene history exactly.
dis.ruled: Cysts are an amoebic feature, and cysts do not lyse collagen.

rules: If a lens wearer has a stromal infiltrate under an epithelial defect, scrape and culture before the first drop. If thinning progresses on hourly cover, fortify and plan for perforation.

title: The eye that has been red twice before
stem: A 41-year-old man has four days of watering, mild photophobia and blur OD, and two similar episodes in the past two years. BVA 20/40 OD. A branching epithelial lesion with terminal bulbs stains with fluorescein, its bed stains faintly with rose bengal, corneal sensation is reduced OD, and two small anterior stromal opacities remain from an earlier episode. Chamber quiet, IOP 16 both eyes.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Herpes zoster pseudodendritic keratopathy
Herpes simplex epithelial keratitis, recurrent
Healing abrasion with a dendritic epithelial ridge
Acanthamoeba radial keratoneuritis, early
Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis

items.why: A branching lesion with terminal bulbs, an ulcer bed that stains with rose bengal, reduced sensation and old anterior stromal scars from earlier episodes make recurrent herpes simplex the answer.

dis.label: Zoster pseudodendrite
dis.tempting: Zoster also gives a raised branching lesion with reduced sensation.
dis.ruled: Pseudodendrites are heaped mucus with no terminal bulbs and no ulcer bed.

dis.label: Healing abrasion
dis.tempting: Healing epithelium forms ridges that can look dendritic on staining.
dis.ruled: A healing ridge has no terminal bulbs, and it does not recur three times.

items.q: What is the most appropriate treatment now?

options.t: Topical ganciclovir 0.15% gel five times daily
Topical ganciclovir gel with dexamethasone twice daily
Oral aciclovir 400 mg twice daily as sole therapy
Preservative-free lubricants and review in one week
Topical chloramphenicol with a bandage contact lens

items.short: Topical ganciclovir gel, five times daily
items.why: Live virus in the epithelium needs an antiviral at treatment dose until the lesion heals. Steroid on a live dendrite drives geographic ulceration, and lubricants do nothing to the virus.

dis.label: Antiviral plus steroid
dis.tempting: Steroid limits the scarring his earlier episodes plainly caused.
dis.ruled: Steroid belongs to stromal disease. On a dendrite it enlarges the ulcer.

dis.label: Oral aciclovir alone
dis.tempting: Oral dosing avoids drop toxicity and reaches the ganglion too.
dis.ruled: 400 mg twice daily is the prophylactic dose, not a treatment dose.

items.q: At two weeks the epithelium is intact but acuity is 20/60 with central stromal haze and cells, and no keratic precipitates. What has happened?

options.t: Antiviral epithelial toxicity with pseudodendrites
Herpetic stromal keratitis without ulceration
Neurotrophic keratopathy from lost sensation
Herpetic endotheliitis with secondary oedema
Bacterial superinfection of a healed dendrite

items.why: Stromal haze with chamber cells appearing after the epithelium has healed is an immune stromal reaction, not live epithelial virus. No defect and no precipitates place the disease in the stroma.

dis.label: Endotheliitis
dis.tempting: Stromal thickening with a chamber reaction is close to its picture.
dis.ruled: Endotheliitis needs keratic precipitates under the oedema. There are none.

dis.label: Antiviral toxicity
dis.tempting: Two weeks of gel five times daily does cause punctate toxicity.
dis.ruled: Toxicity is epithelial and stains. This haze sits under an intact surface.

items.q: Which regimen is most appropriate for this stage?

options.t: Topical prednisolone with antiviral cover, slow taper
Topical prednisolone hourly without antiviral cover
Oral aciclovir 400 mg five times daily as sole therapy
Topical ganciclovir gel five times daily as sole therapy
Topical ciclosporin 0.05% twice daily as sole therapy

items.short: Steroid under antiviral cover, slow taper
items.why: Immune stromal disease needs steroid, and steroid needs antiviral cover to stop epithelial recurrence. Rapid withdrawal produces the rebound that scars the visual axis.

dis.label: Steroid, no cover
dis.tempting: It treats the immune stroma, which is what is costing him vision.
dis.ruled: Unopposed steroid reactivates epithelial virus and risks geographic ulcer.

dis.label: Antiviral alone
dis.tempting: It cleared the dendrite, so continuing it feels consistent.
dis.ruled: Antiviral does not touch the immune infiltrate driving the stromal haze.

items.q: Which two statements about latency and recurrence are correct?

options.t: Latent virus resides in the trigeminal ganglion
Recurrence follows reactivation and axonal transport
Recurrence reflects fresh exogenous reinfection
Corneal sensation recovers fully between episodes
Latency is maintained in corneal stromal keratocytes

items.why: Herpes simplex persists in the trigeminal ganglion and travels down ophthalmic axons when reactivated. Recurrence is endogenous, and sensory loss accumulates with each episode.

dis.label: Exogenous reinfection
dis.tempting: Repeat episodes suggest repeat exposure, as with conjunctivitis.
dis.ruled: Recurrence is reactivation of the patient's own latent virus.

dis.label: Sensation, keratocytes
dis.tempting: Both sound reasonable: nerves recover, keratocytes host stromal disease.
dis.ruled: Sensory loss is cumulative, and latency is ganglionic rather than corneal.

rules: If a branching epithelial lesion has terminal bulbs, treat live virus and hold the steroid. If stromal haze appears after the epithelium heals, add steroid only under antiviral cover.

title: Pain out of proportion to the slit lamp findings
stem: A 27-year-old man rinses his monthly lenses under the tap and swims in them. Three weeks of worsening OS pain, now severe and disturbing sleep, with photophobia and blur. Two courses of topical antiviral and one of a fluoroquinolone have not helped. BVA 20/80 OS. Patchy anterior stromal infiltrates in an incomplete ring, radial perineural infiltrates, epithelial pseudodendrites, limbitis. IOP 18 both eyes.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Herpes simplex stromal keratitis, unresponsive
Acanthamoeba keratitis from tap water exposure
Fungal keratitis with feathery stromal extension
Atypical mycobacterial keratitis after lens trauma
Pseudomonas keratitis, partially treated

items.why: Pain far beyond the visible signs for three weeks, radial perineural infiltrates, a partial ring infiltrate and failure of antiviral and antibacterial therapy in a tap-rinsing swimmer name the amoeba.

dis.label: HSV stromal keratitis
dis.tempting: Pseudodendrites and a chronic course took two clinicians there already.
dis.ruled: Simplex gives neither radial perineural infiltrates nor a ring in weeks.

dis.label: Fungal keratitis
dis.tempting: Also indolent, also unmoved by antibacterials, also lens related.
dis.ruled: Water exposure without vegetable trauma, and no feathery satellite edges.

items.q: Which three findings most strongly separate this from herpes simplex?

options.t: Radial perineural stromal infiltrates
Pain far in excess of the slit lamp signs
An incomplete ring infiltrate in the stroma
Reduced corneal sensation in the affected eye
Epithelial irregularity with pseudodendrites
A unilateral red eye with photophobia

items.why: Radial keratoneuritis, a ring infiltrate and pain out of proportion are amoebic. Reduced sensation, pseudodendrites and unilateral photophobia occur in both and separate nothing.

dis.label: Reduced sensation
dis.tempting: Sensory loss is the herpetic sign every candidate learns first.
dis.ruled: Both diseases blunt sensation, so it cannot tell them apart.

dis.label: Pseudodendrites, redness
dis.tempting: Pseudodendrites are why the antiviral was started twice already.
dis.ruled: Amoebic epithelium mimics dendrites, and redness is common to both.

items.q: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.t: Topical polyhexanide and propamidine, hourly at first
Hourly fortified vancomycin and amikacin drops
Topical prednisolone with the antiviral continued
Therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty within the fortnight
Oral itraconazole with topical natamycin drops

items.why: A biguanide is the agent that kills cysts, and a diamidine added to it covers trophozoites. Intensive hourly dosing in the first days decides whether the ring resolves.

dis.label: Steroid plus antiviral
dis.tempting: It was the working diagnosis, and steroid does settle the limbitis.
dis.ruled: Steroid raises amoebic load and delays cure. Treat the organism first.

dis.label: Early keratoplasty
dis.tempting: Medical therapy is long and the eye is deteriorating week by week.
dis.ruled: Grafting an active amoebic cornea recurs in the graft. Treat first.

items.q: At six weeks the infiltrate has cleared but a sterile ring inflammation persists with acuity 20/100. What now?

options.t: Add topical steroid, continuing the biguanide
Stop the biguanide and start topical steroid
Add oral voriconazole to the biguanide
Restart hourly propamidine for two weeks
Proceed to therapeutic keratoplasty this month

items.why: Inflammation persisting after the organism is controlled is immune, and steroid settles it. The biguanide continues because steroid can wake residual cysts.

dis.label: Steroid, cover stopped
dis.tempting: The infiltrate has cleared, so the anti-amoebic looks finished.
dis.ruled: Cysts survive months. Steroid without cover produces relapse.

dis.label: Keratoplasty now
dis.tempting: 20/100 with a scarred axis looks like a surgical problem.
dis.ruled: Graft an inflamed eye and it fails. Wait for quiescence.

items.q: Which property of the organism explains why treatment runs for months?

options.t: The cyst wall resists drugs and disinfectants
Trophozoites divide faster than epithelium heals
It forms biofilm on the corneal surface
It survives inside keratocytes as a latent form
It seeds the trigeminal nerve and reactivates later

items.why: The double-walled cyst is dormant and poorly permeable, so it outlives short courses and multipurpose solutions. Cure means outlasting cysts, not merely clearing trophozoites.

dis.label: Intracellular latency
dis.tempting: Chronicity and relapse feel like an intracellular hiding place.
dis.ruled: The amoeba is extracellular. It hides in a cyst, not in a cell.

dis.label: Nerve seeding
dis.tempting: Radial perineural infiltrates make the nerves look like a reservoir.
dis.ruled: That infiltrate is inflammation around nerves, not neural latency.

rules: If a lens wearer has pain out of proportion to the signs and no response to antiviral or antibacterial therapy, scrape for amoeba. If steroid is added later, keep the biguanide running.

rows: Severe, out of proportion to the signs
Radial perineural, then an incomplete ring
Tap water, swimming, poor lens hygiene
Previous cold sore or previous dendrite
pair.decider: Radial perineural infiltrates or a ring infiltrate in a lens wearer exposed to water outweigh any pseudodendrite. Scrape and culture for amoeba before more steroid goes in.

title: The teenager whose glasses change at every visit
stem: A 17-year-old boy with atopic eczema rubs his eyes daily. Over 14 months OD refraction moved from -2.75 -1.50 x 175 to -4.00 -3.25 x 160, BVA 20/25. Tomography OD: maximum keratometry 51.8 D, up 1.9 D over those 14 months, thinnest point 442 µm, inferior steepening with a displaced thin point. OS Kmax 46.2 D, unchanged. No scarring, no oedema, endothelium normal.

items.q: Which finding establishes progression?

options.t: Cylinder has increased by 1.75 D with axis rotation
Maximum keratometry has risen 1.9 D in 14 months
The thinnest point measures 442 µm
Inferior steepening with a displaced thin point
Best corrected acuity is still 20/25 in that eye

items.why: Progression is a documented change in corneal shape, most reliably a rise in maximum keratometry with thinning. Refraction varies with fit and effort, and one thin reading is not a change.

dis.label: Thinnest point 442 µm
dis.tempting: A thin cornea is the hallmark of the disease and looks like severity.
dis.ruled: One measurement is a state, not a change. Progression needs two dates.

dis.label: Acuity still 20/25
dis.tempting: Preserved vision reads as reassurance that nothing has moved.
dis.ruled: Acuity holds until the axis distorts. It lags shape by many months.

items.q: What is the most appropriate management?

options.t: Epithelium-off cross-linking OD, monitor OS
Rigid gas permeable fitting OD, no cross-linking
Cross-linking of both eyes at the same session
Repeat tomography in 12 months, then decide
Intrastromal ring segments OD with spectacles

items.short: Cross-link the progressing eye, watch the other
items.why: Cross-linking is indicated by documented progression, and this eye has it at 17 with 442 µm of tissue. The fellow eye is stable, so it is monitored rather than treated.

dis.label: Rigid lens only
dis.tempting: A rigid lens restores the acuity he actually came about.
dis.ruled: A lens corrects the shape, it does not stop the shape changing.

dis.label: Review in 12 months
dis.tempting: Watchful waiting sounds proportionate in a young seeing eye.
dis.ruled: He is already progressing. Another year of steepening costs tissue.

items.q: Which two factors would defer standard epithelium-off cross-linking?

options.t: Stromal thickness under 400 µm after debridement
Active atopic keratoconjunctivitis with lid disease
Maximum keratometry above 50 D
Age 17 rather than over 18
Apical scarring visible on the slit lamp
Corrected acuity better than 20/30

items.why: The standard protocol needs 400 µm of stroma after debridement to protect the endothelium, and an inflamed atopic surface heals badly. A high Kmax and young age argue for treating, not waiting.

dis.label: Age 17
dis.tempting: Consent and cooperation make young age feel like a reason to wait.
dis.ruled: Young eyes progress fastest. Age brings the treatment forward.

dis.label: Kmax 50 D, good acuity
dis.tempting: Both read like thresholds: too steep to treat, too good to risk.
dis.ruled: Neither defers anything. Documented progression is the indication.

items.q: Three months after treatment acuity is 20/60 with central stromal haze and no epithelial defect. What is the most likely cause?

options.t: Microbial keratitis after epithelial removal
Expected post-cross-linking stromal haze
Continued progression despite treatment
Endothelial decompensation from irradiation
Sterile infiltrate from the bandage lens

items.why: Haze at the demarcation line peaks in the first months and clears over a year as acuity recovers. An intact epithelium with no pain and no cells argues against infection and against decompensation.

dis.label: Microbial keratitis
dis.tempting: Debridement plus a bandage lens is a real route to infection.
dis.ruled: Infection brings pain, a defect and cells. None of the three is present.

dis.label: Endothelial failure
dis.tempting: The stroma was 442 µm thick, close to the safety limit.
dis.ruled: Decompensation gives oedema and folds, not isolated stromal haze.

items.q: How does the treatment stiffen the cornea?

options.t: Riboflavin absorbs UVA and new collagen bonds form
UVA denatures collagen and shrinks the stroma thermally
Riboflavin scavenges radicals and prevents enzymatic loss
UVA kills keratocytes so the stroma stops remodelling
Riboflavin blocks UVA from reaching the endothelium

items.why: UVA excites riboflavin, which releases reactive oxygen species and forms covalent bonds between collagen fibrils and proteoglycans. The stiffened stroma resists further steepening.

dis.label: Riboflavin as a shield
dis.tempting: It does shield deeper tissue, which is why the 400 µm rule exists.
dis.ruled: Shielding is a safety effect. Stiffening comes from bond formation.

dis.label: Thermal shrinkage
dis.tempting: Older thermokeratoplasty worked that way, so it sounds familiar.
dis.ruled: These UVA doses are non-thermal. Collagen is bonded, not shrunk.

rules: If maximum keratometry rises with thinning across two dates, cross-link rather than refit. If the stroma measures under 400 µm after debridement, change the protocol, not the indication.

title: The rash that stopped at the middle of the forehead
stem: A 68-year-old woman taking methotrexate has four days of right brow pain, then a vesicular rash over the forehead and upper lid that stops at the midline, with lesions on the tip of the nose. BVA 20/30 OD. Pseudodendritic epithelial plaques, reduced corneal sensation, 1+ cells, a few pigmented keratic precipitates, sectoral iris atrophy. IOP 15 OS, 26 OD. Discs normal.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Primary herpes simplex with a periocular rash
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus with anterior uveitis
Impetiginised contact dermatitis of the lids
Bacterial preseptal cellulitis with lid vesicles
Eczema herpeticum with secondary keratitis

items.why: A painful vesicular rash confined to one dermatome, respecting the midline and involving the nose tip, with sectoral iris atrophy, pigmented precipitates and a raised pressure, is zoster.

dis.label: Primary herpes simplex
dis.tempting: Vesicles and pseudodendrites overlap, and both are herpesviruses.
dis.ruled: Simplex respects no dermatome and does not atrophy the iris in sectors.

dis.label: Preseptal cellulitis
dis.tempting: A hot swollen lid in an immunosuppressed patient reads bacterial.
dis.ruled: Dermatomal vesicles with intraocular signs are not preseptal disease.

items.q: Which antiviral treatment is most appropriate?

options.t: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily, seven days
Oral aciclovir 400 mg five times daily for five days
Topical ganciclovir 0.15% gel five times daily
Intravenous aciclovir for seven days as an inpatient
Oral valaciclovir 500 mg twice daily for five days

items.short: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily
items.why: Zoster needs the higher oral dose five times daily, started as early as possible, to cut ocular complications and neuralgia. Simplex doses undertreat it and topical gel never reaches the skin.

dis.label: Aciclovir 400 mg
dis.tempting: It is the familiar dose carried over from simplex keratitis.
dis.ruled: Varicella zoster is less sensitive and needs twice that dose.

dis.label: Intravenous therapy
dis.tempting: She is immunosuppressed, so parenteral cover feels safer.
dis.ruled: Reserve it for dissemination or encephalitis. She has neither.

items.q: How should the pressure of 26 mmHg in that eye be managed?

options.t: Topical steroid for the uveitis plus a beta-blocker
Topical prostaglandin analogue as first-line control
Observe the pressure until the rash has resolved
Oral acetazolamide 250 mg four times daily
Topical pilocarpine 2% four times daily

items.short: Treat the trabeculitis, add a beta-blocker
items.why: The rise here is trabeculitis, so treating the inflammation lowers it, with aqueous suppression added while it settles. Prostaglandins and miotics aggravate inflammation.

dis.label: Prostaglandin analogue
dis.tempting: It is the strongest single agent and the usual first choice.
dis.ruled: Prostaglandins can worsen uveitis and are avoided while it is active.

dis.label: Pilocarpine
dis.tempting: Miosis and better outflow both sound useful in a pressure spike.
dis.ruled: Miotics increase inflammation and pull the iris into synechiae.

items.q: Which three actions belong in her care over the next month?

options.t: Discuss zoster vaccination once this episode settles
Review at intervals for a year for late stromal disease
Tell her rheumatology team about the acute infection
Stop the methotrexate permanently to prevent recurrence
Prescribe a topical antibiotic for the crusting lesions
Arrange varicella serology to confirm the diagnosis

items.short: Vaccine discussion, long review, inform the team
items.why: Zoster eye disease relapses for years, so review runs long and vaccination is discussed after recovery. Her immunosuppression is a decision for the team that prescribes it.

dis.label: Stop methotrexate
dis.tempting: Immunosuppression allowed reactivation, so stopping looks protective.
dis.ruled: Her joint disease needs it. Any change belongs to the prescriber.

dis.label: Varicella serology
dis.tempting: Laboratory proof feels rigorous before a year of follow-up.
dis.ruled: A dermatomal vesicular rash is the diagnosis. Serology changes nothing.

items.q: She asks whether she can work in a nursery while the rash is active. What is the correct advice?

options.t: Stay away until every lesion has crusted over
Return once oral antiviral therapy has started
Return when the rash is covered by a dressing
No restriction, since zoster is not transmissible
Stay away for 21 days from the rash appearing

items.short: Away from the nursery until lesions crust
items.why: Vesicle fluid transmits varicella to non-immune contacts, and infectivity ends when the lesions crust. Treatment shortens the illness, and a dressing does not remove the duty to stay away.

dis.label: Back once treated
dis.tempting: Antivirals reduce viral shedding, which sounds like safety.
dis.ruled: Shedding continues until crusting. Treatment does not end exclusion.

dis.label: No restriction
dis.tempting: Zoster needs contact, unlike chickenpox spread through the air.
dis.ruled: Vesicle fluid still gives varicella to non-immune children.

rules: If a dermatomal rash reaches the tip of the nose, examine the eye and start high-dose oral antiviral that day. If the pressure rises, treat the trabeculitis rather than adding a prostaglandin.

title: Vision that faded again two years after surgery
stem: A 71-year-old man had uncomplicated phacoemulsification OS 26 months ago and reached 20/20. He now reports 20/50 OS, glare in sunlight and difficulty with print. Refraction is unchanged from his one-month postoperative result. The implant is centred in the bag, with a wrinkled pearly membrane behind it and pearls at its edge. Cornea clear, IOP 16, no cells, macula normal on OCT.

items.q: What is the most likely cause of the drop in vision?

options.t: Pseudophakic cystoid macular oedema
Posterior capsule opacification behind the implant
Late in-the-bag intraocular lens dislocation
Fuchs endothelial dystrophy, decompensating
Refractive change from posterior corneal astigmatism

items.why: A wrinkled pearly membrane with Elschnig pearls behind a centred implant accounts for glare and reduced acuity years after surgery. A normal OCT and stable refraction exclude the alternatives.

dis.label: Pseudophakic CMO
dis.tempting: It is the classic late cause of blur after cataract surgery.
dis.ruled: OCT shows a normal macula, and CMO peaks in months, not two years.

dis.label: Refractive change
dis.tempting: New spectacles are the simplest explanation for gradual blur.
dis.ruled: Refraction is unchanged from one month after his surgery.

items.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.t: Nd:YAG laser posterior capsulotomy in clinic
Surgical membrane peel by a pars plana approach
Intravitreal triamcinolone for the membrane
New spectacles with an anti-glare coating
Lens exchange with polishing of the capsule

items.why: A YAG capsulotomy clears the axis in minutes without entering the eye, and his symptoms justify it. Surgery is kept for a dense fibrotic plate the laser cannot open.

dis.label: Lens exchange
dis.tempting: It removes membrane and pearls together in one definitive operation.
dis.ruled: It trades a two-minute laser for intraocular surgery and its risks.

dis.label: Anti-glare spectacles
dis.tempting: Glare is his main complaint, and coatings genuinely reduce it.
dis.ruled: The scatter is inside the eye. No coating reaches behind the implant.

items.q: Two days after the laser he reports new floaters and a shadow in the upper field. What is the priority?

options.t: Dilated peripheral retinal examination today
Reassurance, since floaters are expected after laser
Measure the pressure and review in one month
Macular OCT to look for postoperative oedema
Repeat the laser to enlarge the opening

items.why: A field shadow with new floaters after capsulotomy is a retinal detachment until proven otherwise, and the laser raises that risk. Only a dilated peripheral view answers the question.

dis.label: Reassure about floaters
dis.tempting: Debris and floaters are genuinely common in the first days.
dis.ruled: A field defect is not debris. The periphery has to be seen today.

dis.label: Macular OCT
dis.tempting: Post-laser oedema is real and OCT is the test that finds it.
dis.ruled: OCT misses the peripheral break causing an upper field shadow.

items.q: Which pressure finding one hour after the laser needs treatment before he leaves?

options.t: Pressure risen from 16 to 31 mmHg
Pressure risen from 16 to 21 mmHg
Pressure unchanged with pigment in the chamber
Pressure fallen to 12 with a shallow chamber
Pressure 18 with a few red cells behind the iris

items.short: A spike to 31 mmHg before discharge
items.why: Pressure peaks in the first hours after capsulotomy as pigment and debris load the outflow. A rise into the thirties is treated and rechecked before he goes home.

dis.label: Rise to 21 mmHg
dis.tempting: It is a rise, and any rise after laser feels like a complication.
dis.ruled: A few points of transient rise is expected and settles untreated.

dis.label: Pigment, same pressure
dis.tempting: Visible pigment is exactly the mechanism of the spike.
dis.ruled: Pigment without a pressure rise needs recheck, not treatment.

items.q: Which two duties apply when consenting him for the laser?

options.t: Disclose the raised risk of retinal detachment
Record that alternatives, including no treatment, were discussed
Obtain consent from a relative as well as from him
Warn him that the implant will be replaced
Guarantee the acuity he had at one month

items.why: Consent covers the material risks a patient in his position would want, detachment and pressure rise among them, and the alternatives including doing nothing. Outcomes are explained, not promised.

dis.label: Relative consents too
dis.tempting: Involving family feels safer for an older patient.
dis.ruled: He has capacity. The consent is his alone to give.

dis.label: Guarantee 20/20
dis.tempting: He reached 20/20 before, so promising it sounds honest.
dis.ruled: A guaranteed outcome is not consent. State the expected range.

rules: If vision falls years after cataract surgery with a clear macula and stable refraction, look behind the implant. If a field shadow follows capsulotomy, dilate and examine the periphery that day.

title: A red aching eye that cannot bear the sunlight
stem: A 29-year-old man has three days of aching OD with photophobia and blur, and six months of early morning low back stiffness that eases as he moves. BVA 20/40 OD. Circumlimbal injection, 3+ cells with 1+ flare, fine keratic precipitates inferiorly, a strand of fibrin, posterior synechiae at 7 o'clock. IOP 11 OD, 15 OS. No vitreous cells, fundus normal. A similar episode affected OS last year.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Herpetic anterior uveitis with trabeculitis
Acute anterior uveitis, HLA-B27 associated
Fuchs uveitis syndrome, first presentation
Intermediate uveitis with anterior spillover
Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis with iritis

items.why: Sudden painful unilateral non-granulomatous inflammation with fibrin, a low pressure and recurrence in the other eye, in a young man with inflammatory back pain, is the B27 pattern.

dis.label: Herpetic uveitis
dis.tempting: It recurs unilaterally too, with fibrin and synechiae of its own.
dis.ruled: Pressure is low, not high, with no sectoral iris atrophy or scar.

dis.label: Intermediate uveitis
dis.tempting: Recurrent uveitis at this age raises it, and spillover is real.
dis.ruled: No vitreous cells and no snowbanks. The reaction is purely anterior.

items.q: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.t: Hourly topical prednisolone 1% with cyclopentolate
Topical prednisolone four times daily with lubricants
Oral prednisolone 40 mg daily with a topical antibiotic
Topical ketorolac four times daily with cyclopentolate
Sub-Tenon triamcinolone injection at this visit

items.why: Three plus cells with fibrin needs intensive topical steroid rather than a four times daily dose, and cycloplegia both eases spasm and breaks the synechiae that are forming.

dis.label: Steroid four times daily
dis.tempting: It is the right drug at a familiar starting frequency.
dis.ruled: Underdosing fibrinous uveitis leaves synechiae behind. Start hourly.

dis.label: Sub-Tenon steroid
dis.tempting: One injection secures delivery and removes any compliance worry.
dis.ruled: Kept for resistant or posterior disease. Drops reach the front.

items.q: Which two features point to a systemic association worth investigating?

options.t: Inflammatory back pain for six months
Recurrence alternating between the eyes
Fine keratic precipitates inferiorly
Intraocular pressure of 11 mmHg
Photophobia with circumlimbal injection

items.why: Morning stiffness that eases with movement suggests axial spondyloarthritis, and recurrent alternating acute anterior uveitis is its ocular signature. The rest occurs in any acute iritis.

dis.label: Fine precipitates
dis.tempting: Precipitate character does separate granulomatous disease.
dis.ruled: Fine precipitates are non-specific and appear in any acute iritis.

dis.label: Low pressure, glare
dis.tempting: Both are abnormal and both belong to the picture in front of you.
dis.ruled: Ciliary hyposecretion and photophobia occur whatever the cause.

items.q: Which referral and test plan fits him best?

options.t: Rheumatology referral, HLA-B27 and sacroiliac imaging
Rheumatology referral with a full autoimmune screen
Chest imaging with serum ACE and calcium
Syphilis and tuberculosis testing before any steroid
No investigation, since first-line therapy is unchanged

items.why: The history points at one disease, so the tests are aimed there rather than scattered. Naming axial disease changes his systemic treatment even though it does not change today's drops.

dis.label: Full autoimmune screen
dis.tempting: Casting wide feels thorough once a systemic cause is suspected.
dis.ruled: Unaimed panels generate false positives and delay the right referral.

dis.label: No investigation
dis.tempting: Treatment today is identical whichever result comes back.
dis.ruled: The result changes his spinal care and his relapse risk, not his drops.

items.q: Which mechanism best explains the low pressure in the inflamed eye?

options.t: Reduced aqueous production by an inflamed ciliary body
Increased outflow through an inflamed trabecular meshwork
Fibrin plugging the trabecular meshwork
Posterior synechiae obstructing the pupil
Reduced episcleral venous pressure from injection

items.why: Inflamed ciliary epithelium secretes less aqueous, so pressure falls despite debris in the meshwork. When pressure rises instead, suspect trabeculitis or a herpetic cause.

dis.label: Fibrin in the meshwork
dis.tempting: Fibrin is visible in this chamber and does obstruct outflow.
dis.ruled: Obstruction raises pressure. This eye is soft, so inflow has fallen.

dis.label: Posterior synechiae
dis.tempting: Pupil block is a familiar pressure mechanism in uveitis.
dis.ruled: Seclusion raises pressure through iris bombe. It does not lower it.

rules: If acute anterior uveitis recurs and alternates in a young adult, ask about inflammatory back pain and refer. If fibrin is present, dose the steroid hourly and dilate the pupil.

title: A boring pain that wakes her at three in the morning
stem: A 54-year-old woman with nine years of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis has 10 days of deep boring OS pain that wakes her, with tenderness on palpation of the globe. BVA 20/30 OS. A violaceous patch of deep injection nasally that does not blanch with topical phenylephrine, an oedematous sclera in daylight, and a 1 mm peripheral corneal gutter with intact epithelium. IOP 14 both eyes.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Nodular episcleritis with adjacent corneal drying
Diffuse anterior scleritis with a corneal gutter
Peripheral ulcerative keratitis without scleritis
Necrotising scleritis with established thinning
Sclerosing keratitis from long-standing dry eye

items.short: Diffuse anterior scleritis with a gutter
items.why: Pain that wakes her, tenderness on palpation, violaceous injection that phenylephrine does not blanch, and an oedematous sclera in daylight define scleritis. The gutter marks corneal involvement.

dis.label: Nodular episcleritis
dis.tempting: Both are red and sectoral, and episcleritis is far commoner.
dis.ruled: Episcleral vessels blanch with phenylephrine and rarely wake anyone.

dis.label: Necrotising scleritis
dis.tempting: Rheumatoid disease is exactly where necrotising scleritis appears.
dis.ruled: No avascular patch and no translucent thinning. The sclera is swollen.

items.q: Which three findings separate this from episcleritis?

options.t: Injection that phenylephrine does not blanch
Pain that wakes her from sleep
Tenderness of the globe on palpation
Sectoral rather than diffuse redness
Watering with mild photophobia
Symptoms present for 10 days

items.short: No blanching, night pain, globe tenderness
items.why: Deep vessels do not blanch, and only scleral inflammation gives boring pain that wakes a patient and tenderness felt through the lid. Sector redness, watering and duration occur in both.

dis.label: Sectoral redness
dis.tempting: Nodular episcleritis is sectoral, so a sector feels diagnostic.
dis.ruled: Both diseases can be sectoral. The plane of the vessels decides.

dis.label: Watering, 10 days
dis.tempting: Symptoms and duration read like markers of severity.
dis.ruled: Episcleritis waters as well, and it can run for several weeks.

items.q: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.t: Oral NSAID with gastric cover, rheumatology review
Topical prednisolone four times daily with lubricants
Oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg starting today
Topical NSAID with a bandage contact lens
Subconjunctival triamcinolone to the affected quadrant

items.short: Oral NSAID with gastric cover, refer
items.why: Non-necrotising scleritis usually answers a full-dose oral NSAID, and topical steroid does not reach the sclera. The corneal gutter and her rheumatoid disease bring in the physician.

dis.label: Topical steroid alone
dis.tempting: Steroid is the reflex anti-inflammatory for a painful red eye.
dis.ruled: Drops do not penetrate to the sclera. This treatment is systemic.

dis.label: Subconjunctival steroid
dis.tempting: It places drug exactly where the inflammation can be seen.
dis.ruled: Avoided where sclera may thin. The perforation risk is real.

items.q: Three weeks later the pain is worse, the gutter is deeper, and an avascular scleral patch has appeared. What now?

options.t: Urgent systemic immunosuppression, shared care
Increase the oral NSAID to the maximum dose
Topical ciclosporin with punctal occlusion
Scleral patch graft before any medical change
Oral prednisolone alone, tapered over four weeks

items.why: An avascular patch with a deepening gutter is necrotising disease, which threatens the globe and signals active systemic vasculitis. Steroid alone relapses, so a steroid-sparing agent starts now.

dis.label: More NSAID
dis.tempting: It is the class that seemed to be controlling her at first.
dis.ruled: Necrotising disease has outrun NSAIDs. Change class, not dose.

dis.label: Patch graft first
dis.tempting: Thinning sclera looks like a structural problem to repair.
dis.ruled: Grafts melt in inflamed sclera. Control the disease, then rebuild.

items.q: Why does the cornea thin at the periphery in this disease?

options.t: Limbal vessels deliver immune complexes and proteases
Tear film breaks up faster over the peripheral cornea
Peripheral cornea is thinner than the centre to begin with
Limbal stem cells fail and the epithelium breaks down
Peripheral stroma holds fewer keratocytes for repair

items.short: Limbal vessels bring complexes and proteases
items.why: The peripheral cornea abuts limbal vessels, so immune complexes deposit there and recruit neutrophils whose proteases digest stroma. The avascular centre is spared.

dis.label: Peripheral thinness
dis.tempting: Anatomy makes it sound as though the thinnest tissue goes first.
dis.ruled: The peripheral cornea is thicker than the centre, not thinner.

dis.label: Tear break-up
dis.tempting: Rheumatoid patients are dry, and dryness does harm epithelium.
dis.ruled: Dryness gives punctate staining, not a vascularised immune gutter.

rules: If a red eye is tender to palpation and the redness does not blanch with phenylephrine, treat it systemically and ask why. If a scleral patch turns avascular, escalate immunosuppression.

rows: Deep and boring, wakes the patient
Gritty or uncomfortable, sleeps through it
Blue-violet hue with an oedematous sclera
Bright red vessels over white sclera
pair.decider: Redness that will not blanch with phenylephrine, in an eye tender to palpation, means scleritis, systemic work-up and systemic treatment rather than a topical prescription.

title: Door frames that started to bend six weeks ago
stem: A 78-year-old woman reports six weeks of distortion OD, with door frames bowed and print she managed in June now hard to read. She smokes 15 cigarettes a day. BVA was 20/25 OD in June and is 20/60 today. Amsler shows central metamorphopsia OD. Fundus OD: soft confluent drusen, a grey-green subretinal lesion and a small subretinal haemorrhage temporal to fixation. OS drusen only, 20/25.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Geographic atrophy involving the foveal centre
Neovascular age-related macular degeneration
Chronic central serous chorioretinopathy
Retinal macroaneurysm with macular exudation
Vitreomacular traction with a lamellar defect

items.why: Six weeks of metamorphopsia with acuity falling from 20/25 to 20/60, a grey-green subretinal lesion, subretinal blood and confluent soft drusen is choroidal neovascularisation on an AMD background.

dis.label: Geographic atrophy
dis.tempting: Same disease and same drusen, and it also destroys reading vision.
dis.ruled: Atrophy is slow, grey-white with visible choroidal vessels, and dry.

dis.label: Chronic CSC
dis.tempting: Subretinal fluid with distortion belongs to its picture too.
dis.ruled: Her age, the drusen and the subretinal blood do not fit CSC.

items.q: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.t: Refer for macular OCT and anti-VEGF within one week
Refer for macular OCT within one week, then observe
Routine referral for assessment in six to eight weeks
Start high-dose antioxidant supplements and review
Refer for focal laser photocoagulation of the lesion

items.short: Urgent referral for OCT and anti-VEGF
items.why: Vision lost to active neovascularisation returns only if injections start within days to weeks. Imaging and treatment are arranged on one pathway rather than one after the other.

dis.label: Routine referral
dis.tempting: Six weeks feels prompt measured against usual waiting times.
dis.ruled: Fibrosis is permanent. Each week of delay costs recoverable acuity.

dis.label: Antioxidant supplements
dis.tempting: Supplements do have trial evidence in age-related disease.
dis.ruled: They lower risk in the fellow eye. They do not treat active disease.

items.q: Which three belong in her care alongside the injections?

options.t: Smoking cessation support offered at this visit
Amsler self-monitoring of the fellow eye
Low vision assessment and reading aids
A supplement containing beta-carotene
Surrender of her driving licence this week
Laser prophylaxis to drusen in the fellow eye

items.short: Stop smoking, Amsler the fellow eye, low vision aids
items.why: Smoking is her one modifiable risk, the fellow eye needs a home test that catches conversion early, and reading aids restore function while treatment runs.

dis.label: Beta-carotene formula
dis.tempting: It resembles the supplement trial she may have read about.
dis.ruled: Beta-carotene raises lung cancer risk in smokers. Use the later formula.

dis.label: Surrender the licence
dis.tempting: Central loss in one eye reads like the end of driving.
dis.ruled: OS is 20/25. She is assessed against the standard, not disqualified.

items.q: After three monthly injections OD is 20/40 with a little persistent subretinal fluid. What now?

options.t: Continue injections and set the treatment interval
Stop injections and monitor with monthly OCT
Switch to a different anti-VEGF agent today
Add photodynamic therapy to the next injection
Extend to four-monthly injections immediately

items.short: Continue injections, then titrate the interval
items.why: Acuity improved and fluid is reducing, which is a response. Treatment continues while the interval is titrated to the eye, because stopping after loading invites recurrence.

dis.label: Stop and monitor
dis.tempting: Three injections is the loading course, so it sounds complete.
dis.ruled: Loading starts therapy. Fluid remains, so injections continue.

dis.label: Switch the agent
dis.tempting: Persistent fluid reads as failure of the drug in use.
dis.ruled: This eye improved. Switching is for non-response, not partial response.

items.q: Which process most directly produces the leakage in this eye?

options.t: VEGF driven vessel growth through Bruch membrane
Lipofuscin accumulation in the pigment epithelium
Choriocapillaris dropout with photoreceptor loss
Vitreous traction on the internal limiting membrane
Complement activation forming drusen deposits

items.short: VEGF driven growth through Bruch membrane
items.why: Hypoxic, inflamed outer retina raises VEGF, which drives choroidal vessels through breaks in Bruch membrane. Those new vessels are permeable, so fluid and blood collect under the retina.

dis.label: Complement and drusen
dis.tempting: Complement is central to the disease and drusen are visible here.
dis.ruled: It explains the background, not the leaking vessel in front of you.

dis.label: Lipofuscin build-up
dis.tempting: It underlies the pigment epithelial ageing that starts all this.
dis.ruled: Lipofuscin drives atrophy over years, not acute subretinal fluid.

rules: If distortion is new and acuity has fallen with a grey-green lesion or subretinal blood, refer for injection within days. If fluid persists while vision improves, continue and titrate.

rows: Older, soft drusen in both eyes
Often Asian ethnicity, fewer soft drusen
Orange-red nodules at the posterior pole
Fluid on OCT, leakage on angiography
pair.decider: Recurrent large haemorrhage or orange nodules justify indocyanine green angiography, because polypoidal disease may need photodynamic therapy as well as anti-VEGF.
